questions.prompt: The KEY philosophical difference between CSMA/**CA** and CSMA/**CD**:
options: CA AVOIDS collisions before sending (DIFS, early random backoff, ACKs, RTS/CTS) because it cannot detect them; CD detects mid-transmission and recovers (abort + jam + backoff)
CA detects collisions faster than CD
CD is for wireless, CA for wired
CA needs no backoff at all
questions.explain:
**CD** (wired): listen WHILE transmitting → abort early + jam + binary exponential backoff.
**CA** (wireless): cannot detect → **avoid**: wait DIFS, random backoff BEFORE sending even when idle, require **ACKs** (after SIFS), optionally reserve with **RTS/CTS**.
vs pure CSMA: CSMA transmits through a collision wasting the whole frame time.

questions.prompt: A laptop joins a WLAN passively. The correct sequence of what it RECEIVES/SENDS is:
options: Receives beacons (SSID + AP MAC) → sends Association Request → receives Association Response → DHCP exchange
Sends beacons → receives Probe → sends DHCP Offer
Sends Association Response → receives beacon → ARP
Receives Probe Request → sends beacon → DHCP
questions.explain: Passive scanning = listen for **beacons** (AP broadcasts SSID + MAC). Then **Association Request** → **Association Response** → **DHCP** (D-O-R-A) to obtain an IP. (Active scanning would start with the host's own Probe Request instead.)

questions.prompt: A frame travels FROM router R1 THROUGH the AP TO wireless host H1. Address 1 / 2 / 3 of the 802.11 frame (AP→H1 leg) are:
options: A1 = H1 (receiver), A2 = AP (transmitter), A3 = R1 (wired-side source)
A1 = AP, A2 = H1, A3 = R1
A1 = R1, A2 = AP, A3 = H1
A1 = H1, A2 = R1, A3 = AP
questions.explain: Same rules, reversed direction: **A1 = receiver of this wireless transmission (H1)**, **A2 = transmitter (AP)**, **A3 = the wired-side node (R1)** so H1 knows the frame's true origin link. The AP is a relay between two links — that's why three addresses exist at all.

questions.prompt: The **triangle routing problem** in mobile IP refers to:
options: Indirect routing detours every datagram correspondent → home network → mobile, inefficient when both are in the same visited network
Three routers forming a forwarding loop
RTS, CTS and DATA forming a triangle
The home agent sending to three foreign agents
questions.explain: Indirect routing: B → home agent → (tunnel to COA) → foreign agent → A. The detour via home is the **triangle**. **Direct routing** fixes it (B learns the COA once, sends straight) at the cost of transparency + anchor-agent chaining when A moves again.

questions.prompt: A 3G user's **voice call** to a landline follows:
options: Mobile → Node B → RNC → MSC → Gateway MSC → public telephone network
Mobile → Node B → RNC → SGSN → GGSN → telephone network
Mobile → RNC → GGSN → Internet → VoIP
Mobile → MSC → Node B → telephone network
questions.explain: Voice rides the (unchanged) **circuit core**: radio leg (UTRAN: mobile → Node B → **RNC**) then **MSC → GMSC** → PSTN. Data forks at the RNC into **SGSN → GGSN → Internet**. Two parallel cores, one radio access network.

questions.prompt: Order the **handoff** steps when a mobile on a call moves to a new base station (same MSC):
items: Old BSS tells the MSC a handoff is needed (names candidate new BSS)
MSC sets up the path/resources to the new BSS
New BSS allocates a radio channel and signals ready
Old BSS tells the mobile: perform handoff; mobile activates the new channel
MSC reroutes the call and releases old-BSS resources
questions.explain: Old BSS initiates → MSC prepares path → new BSS allocates channel → mobile switches → **MSC reroutes + cleanup**. Triggers worth quoting: stronger signal at new BSS, load balancing. The call never drops — design goal.

questions.prompt: Hidden terminal vs fading — what distinguishes them?
options: Hidden terminal = out of range/obstacle blocks sensing; fading = signals too ATTENUATED to sense each other yet still collide at the receiver
They are two names for the same effect
Fading only happens at night
Hidden terminal is a routing problem, fading a transport problem
questions.explain: Both end the same way (undetectable collision at B), but the cause differs: **hidden terminal** = A and C physically cannot hear each other (range/obstacle); **fading** = the A↔C signal exists but is too weak at each other's location, while both remain strong enough at B to interfere. Exam wants both named + the sketch.

questions.prompt: Why does 802.11 use link-layer **ACKs** when Ethernet does not?
options: A wireless sender cannot detect collisions/loss at the receiver (hidden terminals, fading), so explicit confirmation after SIFS is the only way to know the frame arrived
Wireless frames are more valuable
ACKs synchronize the clocks of the stations
It is required by DHCP
questions.explain: Wired CSMA/CD senders KNOW when a collision happens — wireless senders don't (own-signal swamping + hidden terminals). Hence the receiver confirms every good frame with an **ACK after SIFS**; a missing ACK triggers backoff + retransmission. This is the standard 'why ACK' 2-marker.

questions.prompt: Name the process when a mobile's base station changes mid-call (one word).
questions.explain: **Handoff** (also written handover) — old BSS → MSC → new BSS channel allocation → mobile switches → MSC reroutes. Two triggers: stronger signal, load balancing.
